Tubingen
tyoo'bing-en
n. (Wurttemberg university founded 1477; home of Brenz, Jakob Andreae and the Swabian Christology)
From Old High German Tuwingen, of uncertain sense; German Tubingen.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Tubingen trained the theologians of Wurttemberg and through them shaped Lutheran Christology. Johannes Brenz and Jakob Andreae taught there; Andreae was the chief architect of the Formula of Concord of 1577, and the Swabian doctrine of the communication of attributes — that the human nature of Christ truly receives the divine majesty — was framed in its lecture rooms. Two centuries later the same university housed the most destructive school of historical criticism in Europe, which denied what its own forefathers had defended. The dictionary records Tubingen with both facts in view, because an institution does not keep a confession by inheriting one. The doctrine the first Tubingen defended is the doctrine the dictionary holds: one Person in two natures, truly God and truly man. “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (Joh 1:14), and in that flesh “dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines incarnation as the act of assuming flesh and taking a human body and the nature of man, nature as the essential attributes which constitute a thing what it is, and fulness as the state of being filled so as to leave no part vacant.

expand to see more

INCARNA'TION, n. The act of clothing with flesh; the act of assuming flesh, or of taking a human body and the nature of man.

NATURE, n. The essence, essential qualities or attributes of a thing, which constitute it what it is.

FUL'NESS, n. The state of being filled, so as to leave no part vacant; abundance.

FORM, n. A model to be imitated; a prescribed mode or order; a pattern.

Col 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

Php 2:7 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:"

Heb 2:14 — "Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;"

Modern Corruption

The Wurttemberg university of Brenz and Andreae, where the Formula of Concord and the Swabian Christology were framed.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is the one the later Tubingen school produced: a critical method that treated the incarnation as the church's developing idea rather than an event, and the Gospels as deposits of that idea. The dictionary names that method as what it is, and notes that it grew in the very place that had defended the doctrine it dissolved.

The principle to recover is the Chalcedonian confession, one Person and two natures, united without confusion, change, division or separation. The incarnation is an act and not an idea: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (Joh 1:14). The deity is not diminished by it: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9). The humiliation is real and voluntary — He “took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men” (Php 2:7) — and it was undertaken for a purpose no idea could accomplish: “that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death” (Heb 2:14).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sarx (G4561), flesh; Greek pleroma (G4138), fulness.

Greek skenoo (G4637) — to pitch a tent, to dwell among; John 1:14.

Greek monogenes (G3439) — only begotten, uniquely of the Father; John 1:14.

Greek pleroma (G4138) — fulness, that which fills completely; Colossians 2:9.

Greek theotes (G2320) — deity, the divine essence itself; Colossians 2:9.

Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty, to make of no reputation; Philippians 2:7.

Usage

"“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (Joh 1:14) — Brenz and Andreae in the Wurttemberg chairs."

"“all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9) — the Formula of Concord, 1577."

"“took upon him the form of a servant” (Php 2:7) — and the later school that dissolved what the first defended."
